GRADE 2 · INCHWORMS / GRIP & MOTION

A loop goes somewhere.

How does an inchworm turn a loop into a step?

FOUR LITTLE WONDERS

Where shall we look?

Choose a question. Look for a clue in the picture, then test your first idea against the explanation.

01Why does the middle rise into a loop?↗02What holds on while the head reaches?↗03How could a leaf vein show it moved?↗04Will this caterpillar always crawl?↗

Start with one question. A question is enough.

LOOK CLOSELY · 01

Why does the middle rise into a loop?

Find the head at the right. Follow the body back to the rear feet. Where is there empty space underneath?

A little explanation & something to try

The front legs hold the leaf while the rear comes closer. The long middle bends upward into a loop. Inchworms have jointed legs near the head and fleshy gripping parts called prolegs near the rear, with a long gap between. They do not walk on a row of legs along that middle.

Try this. Draw a long curved line with its two ends close together. Imagine the front end stays in one place as the rear comes closer. Which part must bend?

LOOK CLOSELY · 02

What holds on while the head reaches?

The front is lifted. Trace the body to the far left. Which feet still touch the leaf?

A little explanation & something to try

Now the rear prolegs anchor the body: they hold it in place. The front reaches ahead as the middle straightens. When the front legs grip again, the rear can catch up. The two ends take turns holding on. That repeating sequence carries the caterpillar across a leaf.

Try this. Point to the rear grip. Predict what might happen if it slipped while the front was still reaching. Use a detail from the picture to explain.

LOOK CLOSELY · 03

How could a leaf vein show it moved?

Compare the two leaf sketches. Each dot records the head. Find the same Y-shaped vein fork in both. What changed?

A little explanation & something to try

A bent body alone does not tell us how far the animal traveled. The first head mark is before the fork; the later mark is beyond it. The fork is a reference point, a place to compare positions against. Those changed positions are evidence for movement. They do not tell us its speed without times.

Try this. Draw a Y and put a dot before it. Draw the same Y again with a dot beyond it. Explain how the two drawings support the idea that the head moved.

LOOK CLOSELY · 04

Will this caterpillar always crawl?

Find three life stages in the notebook. How does the last shape differ from the first?

A little explanation & something to try

An inchworm is a caterpillar, the young stage of a geometer moth. It grows, becomes a pupa, then changes into a moth. This big change in body form is metamorphosis. It takes time; this scene imagines a later stage. A moth has six jointed legs. The caterpillar's fleshy prolegs do not remain.

Try this. Follow the notebook arrows: caterpillar, pupa, moth. Name one body feature that changes. What extra observation would help you learn how long the change takes?

A STORY TO EXPLORE

A loop goes somewhere.

A green arch rises. A head reaches. Follow the tiny grips that carry an inchworm across a leaf.

One little page at a time.

A traveling arch

A traveling arch

A green arch rises on a leaf. “A tiny bridge!” says Little. Then the arch flattens and the head reaches ahead. Big watches beside the path. This is an inchworm, a kind of caterpillar. How can bending help it get somewhere?

Keep a first guess. Which parts touch the leaf?

The rear catches up

The rear catches up

The front legs grip the leaf. The rear comes closer, lifting the long middle into a loop. Near the rear are fleshy grips called prolegs. “No walking legs under that middle!” Little notices. With its ends closer, the body must bend.

Which end holds still while the loop rises?

A grip, then a reach

A grip, then a reach

Now the prolegs anchor the rear: they hold it in place. The front reaches ahead as the body straightens. Once the front grips, the rear can catch up again. “One end holds while the other moves,” Little says. A loop becomes a journey.

Predict what could happen if the rear grip slipped during the reach.

The leaf keeps a clue

The leaf keeps a clue

Little sketches the head before a vein fork, then beyond it. The changed positions are evidence: clues that can support an idea. “It traveled past the fork!” That is an inference, an idea drawn from clues. The same leaf vein makes the comparison fair.

Why is a changed head position stronger evidence than just a bent body?

A pretend leaf journey

A pretend leaf journey

“Does every loop go one inch?” Little asks. The name sounds like measuring, but real steps vary. Little draws a pretend route instead. Its distances are invented. A model helps answer a math question without pretending the leaf picture is a ruler.

What would you need to measure a real journey?

A later shape

A later shape

Little imagines a later chapter. The caterpillar becomes a pupa, then changes into a moth. This change of body form is metamorphosis. It takes time. Little sketches the stages. “A new shape after all those loops!”

Which stage comes between caterpillar and moth?

For grown-ups & print downloads

These are imagined, enlarged scenes, not an identified species or exact leg-count diagrams. Inchworms are geometer moth caterpillars, not earthworms. They generally have three pairs of jointed front legs and two or three pairs of rear prolegs, with a long legless middle; details vary. Tiny hooks on prolegs help grip. Front legs anchor during looping; rear prolegs anchor during extension. Caterpillar, pupa and moth are stages separated by time; timing varies. The pictured winged moth is a possible adult form, though some females have reduced or absent wings. Most inchworms eat plant material, often leaves. The name suggests measuring, not exactly one-inch steps. Compare the same head against the same vein; position evidence alone gives no speed. All millimeter distances are invented and independent of loop count or art scale. Observe a leaf in place if desired; handling or raising animals is unnecessary. Support pronunciation, invented spelling or dictation as useful. Keep adult guidance in this key or collapsed details.

About 15 minutes. Support pronunciation when useful, then let Leo revisit a picture and explain the mechanism. Evidence and inference are deliberately a small step beyond a basic sequence retell. All kid-facing directions address Leo; the same story appears on screen, Letter and foldable.
